newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine fiscal balance needed as debt costs grow.
newsitem.headline: Argentine fiscal balance needed as debt costs grow.

text.p: Argentina's large debt servicing costs next year mean the implementation of the government's tax hiking measures to plug the budget deficit are even more crucial, analysts said.
"Any deviation from the right policy could be a problem," said Esteban Thomsen, Argentina economist at ING Barings.
Net debt service costs will rise to $15.335 billion in 1997 from $11.667 billion this year according to calculations by private consultancy Broda Group.

Juan Arranz, Argentina economist at Santander Investment, calculates that $10.1 billion of next year's payments will be principal redemptions while the remaining $5.2 billion will be used to pay interest.

"Should ministers fail to address the deficit, concerns about solvency would rise and country risk and domestic interest rates would climb which in turn would raise private sector borrowing costs," Arranz said in an investor note.
Therefore, next year's payments "are not much higher (than 1996), but they are important," he added.
The Economy Ministry has estimated it will save between $4 billion and $4.5 billion in 1997 from the tax hikes it hopes to introduce through its latest economic proposals.

"Economy Minister Roque Fernandez's strategy is to tackle the fiscal gap immediately, in order to narrow the 1997 fiscal deficit to $1 billion," said Arranz. The Ministry estimated this year's deficit will be $5 billion.

Should Congress fail to pass the required measures, the debt crunch will be harder to deal with, agrees Agustin Etchebarne, chief economist at private consultancy C&E Consultores. He expects some $6 billion of debt to be issued next year but without the measures another $3 billion will be required.
Another $3.5 billion could be raised if the government sells some of its remaining stake in oil company YPF and through the planned privatization of the Yacyreta hydro-electric dam, said Etchebarne.
So far this year, the government has issued $7 billion of debt and it has proposed to raise another $4 billion through the remainder of the year.

An analyst at a large Argentine bank suggests attention on next year's debt servicing costs could become all the more important for markets because Mexico's interest payments in 1997 are also much higher than this year.
In 1998, Argentina's debt servicing charges fall back down to $13.697 billion, just below this year's levels, according to the Broda Group estimates.
